\begin{abstract}
Kolmogorov--Arnold networks (KANs) are promoted as interpretable because each edge carries a learned univariate function. We show that a widely used family of smoothness penalties leaves a blind spot that undermines this promise: second-difference and curvature penalties do not charge for affine components of an edge, and SiLU base weights are often unpenalised. When the inputs to a trained nonlinear layer are correlated, affine components on different edges can cancel, so training inflates the parameters along directions that neither the penalty nor the data can see, and independent runs do not agree. In pre-registered experiments with a known teacher, correlated inputs gave 0 of 16 converged models, including under a recently proposed curvature penalty, while a small penalty on the affine null space gave 16 of 16 certified minima and essentially exact recovery of the teacher. Along certified regularisation paths spanning five decades, the loss behaves as if its infimum lies at infinity, on synthetic data and on real electrolyte-conductivity data; closing the null space bounds it. Non-convergence rises with input correlation, and the runaway and its fix carry over from Gaussian-RBF to B-spline edges. On the real data, polishing beyond early stopping degraded predictions for a held-out co-solvent (RMSE 0.142 $\to$\allowbreak{} 1.03 under a weak null-space penalty; 0.33 under a stronger one). Certified minima can still be degenerate or distinct, so convergence and identifiability are separate problems. We give practical recommendations for penalised KANs.

\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:1}

KANs replace a network's fixed activations with learned univariate functions on every edge. Their appeal for science rests on reading those functions: an edge that looks like an exponential decay suggests a physical law. That reading presumes the edges are determined by the data. If different training runs produce different edges with equally good predictions, the edges describe the optimiser, not the system.

This paper identifies a concrete, common mechanism that breaks that presumption. It arises from the interaction of three ingredients that are each standard in practice:

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{A smoothness penalty with an affine null space.} Second-difference (P-spline) penalties and curvature penalties ignore straight-line components of an edge; SiLU base terms are frequently unpenalised.
  \item \textbf{Correlated inputs to a layer.} Physical descriptors often move together. Hidden units can also become correlated during training, exposing the next layer.
  \item \textbf{Training toward convergence.} Early stopping hides the problem; longer optimisation exposes it.
\end{enumerate}

Together they create directions along which edges grow into large, mutually cancelling affine shapes. The penalty does not see them, and on the training data their contributions cancel. The loss keeps decreasing slightly along these directions, and over the range we could test it behaves as if it had no finite minimum. Seeds wander apart, no model certifies as converged, and on inputs off the training correlation pattern the cancellation fails.

\textbf{Contributions.}

\begin{itemize}
  \item We describe the mechanism: a penalty's affine blind spot plus correlated inputs to a trained nonlinear layer. A layer whose output is linear in its parameters cannot run away (Sections 3 and 6).
  \item In a pre-registered synthetic study, a recently proposed curvature penalty does not prevent the runaway on correlated inputs, while a small penalty on the affine null space does and restores recovery of a known solution (Section 4).
  \item On real electrolyte-conductivity data, we trace a complete failure to converge to this mechanism and document its effect on a held-out co-solvent (Section 5).
  \item Along certified regularisation paths, the loss behaves as if its infimum lies at infinity over five decades of regularisation, on synthetic and real data; closing the null space bounds it (Section 6).
  \item Non-convergence rises with input correlation, and the runaway and its fix carry over from Gaussian-RBF to B-spline edges (Sections 7 and 8).
  \item Certified minima can be degenerate, distinct or not minima at all; we separate three kinds of flatness and give recommendations (Sections 9 and 10).
\end{itemize}

All experiments were pre-registered: predictions, thresholds and interpretation rules were committed before the code that tested them. Of 65 predictions in the real-data case study, 11 held, 22 failed and 32 were inconclusive; we report them as recorded. The revision studies of Sections 6--8 and the applicability analysis followed the same protocol; Appendix A lists their verdicts, and Appendix D every change made after an outcome was known.

\section{Background and related work}\label{sec:2}

\textbf{KAN edges.} A KAN layer maps inputs to outputs by summing learned univariate functions, one per edge. In the original formulation \citep{liu2025kan} each edge is a SiLU base term plus a B-spline expansion. FastKAN \citep{li2024fastkan} approximates the B-splines with Gaussian radial basis functions on fixed centres, which is the edge type used in our experiments:

\begin{equation}
  \varphi(x) = \alpha\,\mathrm{SiLU}(x) + \sum_{k=1}^{K} c_k \exp\!\left(-\left(\frac{x-\mu_k}{h}\right)^{2}\right)
\end{equation}

\textbf{Smoothness penalties and their null spaces.} P-spline penalties charge squared second differences of the coefficients \citep{eilers1996psplines}. Constant and linear coefficient patterns cost nothing: the penalty's null space is affine. In generalised additive models this is well understood, and \citet{marra2011double} proposed an additional penalty on the null space (the "double penalty") for variable selection; \citet{wood2017gam} treats null spaces and concurvity in additive models in depth. Our fix is the same construction; what is new is its consequence inside a KAN, where edges are summed within units and passed through further layers.

\textbf{Curvature penalties for KANs.} \citet{bagrow2026curvature} proposed per-edge curvature penalties for compositional smoothness, combining the second-difference penalty with a term $K_{\mathrm{silu}}\,\alpha^{2}$ on the SiLU weight, and noted that the penalty has affine functions as its null space by design. That work evaluated on independent, uniformly sampled inputs. Second-derivative penalties on spline coefficients also appear in other KAN variants, typically on the spline part only, leaving the SiLU base term free (\citealp{cang2024kanwork}; see also the free-knots KAN of \citealp{zheng2025freeknots}). We show that the affine null space becomes a runaway direction when inputs are correlated, and that penalising the SiLU weight alone does not close it.

\textbf{Concurvity.} In additive models, including neural additive models \citep{agarwal2021nam}, correlated inputs let one input's shape function absorb another's, making shape functions non-identifiable; this is known as concurvity. \citet{siems2023concurvity} proposed a regulariser penalising correlations between transformed features. The cross-edge cancellation we describe is concurvity inside a KAN unit. In an additive model with a penalised null space it shifts shape between functions; combined with an unpenalised affine null space in a KAN, it becomes unbounded growth.

\textbf{Losses without a finite minimum.} When a loss attains its infimum only at infinity, gradient descent drives the parameter norm to diverge, slowly, and optimisation can continue while held-out performance worsens \citep{soudry2018implicit}. Our runaway behaves like an instance of this, created by a penalty's null space. It differs from the benign flat directions of linear least squares, where gradient descent converges to the minimum-norm solution: here the direction is slightly tilted, so gradient descent keeps following it. On such ill-conditioned problems, early stopping acts much like ridge regularisation \citep{yao2007early,ali2019continuous}.

\textbf{Parameter-space symmetries.} Exact symmetries (unit permutations, sign flips) make parameters non-identifiable in tanh and RBF networks, and completeness results characterise them \citep{sussmann1992uniqueness,kurkova1994uniqueness}. KANs add continuous symmetries such as affine reparametrisations of hidden units. The runaway is not an exact symmetry: it is an approximate one, a nearly flat but tilted direction, which is what prevents convergence.

\section{Mechanism}\label{sec:3}

Consider a unit that sums edges from two inputs, $s = \varphi_1(x_1) + \varphi_2(x_2)$, each edge as in Section 2, trained with a second-difference penalty on its RBF coefficients.

\textbf{Step 1: a direction the penalty cannot see.} Add a linear pattern $t\,\ell$ to the RBF coefficients of edge 1 and subtract it from edge 2, with $\ell_k$ proportional to the centre index. Linear coefficient patterns have zero second difference, so the penalty is unchanged for every t (Figure~\ref{fig:mechanism}b). With Gaussian bumps on a regular grid, the pattern produces a nearly affine function: over the central 80\% of the input range it deviates from a straight line by at most 2\% of its range (Figure~\ref{fig:mechanism}a), and by up to 13\% near the grid edges. Edge 1 thus gains approximately $t\,a\,x_1$ and edge 2 loses $t\,a\,x_2$.

\textbf{Step 2: a direction the data cannot see.} The unit's pre-activation changes by approximately $t\,a\,(x_1 - x_2)$. If $x_{1}$ and $x_{2}$ are strongly correlated, $x_1 - x_2$ is small wherever the data lie, so predictions change little even for large t (Figure~\ref{fig:mechanism}c). The direction is nearly free in both the penalty and the data.

\textbf{Step 3: a receding minimum.} "Nearly free" is not "free". Moving along the direction lets the model shed curvature into the free affine and SiLU components, so the loss keeps decreasing slightly. Both terms contribute (post-hoc decomposition): in the synthetic runaway models the smoothness penalty fell to about a quarter of its early value and supplied a median 61\% of the decrease while training error fell only 5\%; on real data, from early stopping to the capped state, the penalty fell 8--88$\times$ and supplied 17--36\% of the decrease, the data term the rest. The growth went into whatever the penalty left free: the linear part of the RBF coefficients grew 34--40$\times$ in the synthetic runaway cells, and the SiLU weights 85$\times$ where they were unpenalised. In 12 of 20 synthetic runaway models, training error fell while test error rose. Over the range we could test, the loss behaves as if its infimum lies at infinity: along a certified L2 regularisation path, the minimisers grow without levelling off over five decades of the regularisation weight while the loss keeps falling, and they recede along a curved valley rather than a straight ray (Section 6). Growth alone is not the signature, because a distant finite minimum also produces large growth (Step 4); what distinguishes the runaway is that the optimisation never reaches a certified minimum. Different seeds drift along different such directions.

\textbf{Step 4: the runaway needs a trained nonlinear layer.} If the parameters being trained enter the output linearly, as in the output layer when the hidden activations are held fixed, or in a one-layer KAN, the penalised loss is a convex quadratic. It may have flat directions, but no tilted ones, so it cannot run away: with the first layer frozen, every model reached a certified finite minimum, and so did a one-layer model on correlated inputs, although the minimum could lie far away (growth up to $\times$583 on real data). The runaway therefore needs trained parameters that act through a nonlinearity. Correlation can reach such a layer from correlated inputs, or from hidden units that become correlated during training, so the output layer can host the runaway even when the raw inputs are independent, as long as the first layer also adapts. Correlated hidden units are necessary but not sufficient: they also occur in models that converge once the null space is penalised. Whether a given nonlinear problem degenerates depends on the data: with the second layer frozen, the synthetic first-layer problems settled cleanly, while the real first-layer problem, with few-valued, strongly correlated descriptors, reached only highly degenerate minima, one of which was not a minimum at all.

\textbf{Consequences.}

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Non-identifiability:} edges differ across seeds by large affine components that leave predictions almost unchanged; even certified minima can be degenerate or distinct from one another.
  \item \textbf{Non-convergence:} second-order optimisers stall and certification fails. Since growth is also large on the way to a distant finite minimum, certification, not growth, is the criterion.
  \item \textbf{Extrapolation risk:} on inputs outside the training data's support, the inflated components need not cancel. In our real-data case, polishing damaged predictions for a held-out co-solvent lying outside the training descriptor hull.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The fix.} Penalise the null space directly. For each edge, let $P_{\mathrm{null}}$ project its RBF coefficients onto constant-plus-linear patterns in the centre index, and add

\begin{equation}
  Q = \sum_{e} \lVert P_{\mathrm{null}}\, c_e \rVert^{2}
\end{equation}

with a small weight $\mu$, in addition to a penalty on the SiLU weight. This makes every affine component cost something, so the regularised minimisers stay bounded. Penalising only part of the free directions is not enough: the growth moves into whatever stays unpenalised, such as biases or embeddings, so these need a small penalty too.

\section{Controlled study}\label{sec:4}

\textbf{Design.} A teacher KAN [4, 3, 1] with smooth, hand-specified edges (fitted by smoothness-penalised least squares) generates targets with Gaussian noise of 5\% of the output spread; n = 2000 training rows. Inputs are $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)/3$, clipped to the grid, either independent or correlated in pairs ($\rho$ = 0.95 for $x_1/x_2$ and $x_3/x_4$). Students share the teacher's architecture and are trained under three penalty levels:

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{P0:} second-difference penalty on RBF coefficients ($\lambda$ = $10^{-3}$).
  \item \textbf{P1:} P0 plus $K_{\mathrm{silu}}\,\alpha^{2}$ on each SiLU weight (Bagrow-style curvature penalty, $K_{\mathrm{silu}}$ = 0.443).
  \item \textbf{P2:} P1 plus $\mu Q$, the affine null-space penalty.
\end{itemize}

Each of the 6 cells has 8 seeds. Each student is trained with AdamW and early stopping, then polished with an exact-Hessian trust-region method and certified by a second-order criterion (gradient, curvature and Newton decrement). $\mu$ was calibrated before the experiment by a pre-registered rule: $10^{-6}$ failed the pilot (5.0$\times$ growth) and $10^{-5}$ passed (1.32$\times$) and was frozen.

\textbf{The teacher itself runs away.} Polished under P0 and P1 on correlated inputs, the teacher's parameters grew 85$\times$ and 1069$\times$ without certifying, while its predictions stayed within half a noise standard deviation of the original. The runaway changes the parameters, not the function.

\textbf{Results.}

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{The published-style penalty does not prevent the runaway.} Penalising the SiLU weight (P1) halved the growth on correlated inputs but left 0 of 8 models certified (Figure~\ref{fig:synthetic}).
  \item \textbf{Closing the null space prevents it everywhere.} P2 gave 16 of 16 certified models with no growth, in both input conditions.
  \item \textbf{Without the runaway, the internals are recoverable.} Every cell without a runaway matched the reference's units and edges exactly (1.000), with seed-to-seed differences around $10^{-4}$.
  \item \textbf{Independent inputs are not fully safe.} Under P0 and P1, most independent seeds grew substantially (8--12$\times$) but settled at certified minima; 4 of 16 (seeds 0 and 4 in each cell) never certified.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Where the runaway lives.} A post-hoc anatomy of the parameter change shows that in the correlated cells almost all growth sits in the output layer: the layer-1 share of the change was 0.110 (P0) and 0.024 (P1) (Figure~\ref{fig:where}a). The two uncertified independent-P0 seeds put 99.4\% of their change into the output layer. This is Step 4 of Section 3. Among independent-input models, those that ran away were exactly those whose hidden units had become correlated (largest pairwise correlation 0.70, against 0.05 for certified models; Figure~\ref{fig:where}b), while certified P2 models kept correlations up to 0.88 without running away (post-hoc).

\textbf{Verdicts.} Of six pre-registered predictions, one held (the certification pattern, X2) and five failed. The failures refine rather than contradict the mechanism. Independent cells exceeded the growth threshold, mostly through finite growth. Cancellation and extrapolation effects were weaker than predicted. Recoverability failed only because the runaway cells were more recoverable than predicted, not less. In this synthetic setting, polishing did not degrade extrapolation: most of the off-pattern error in correlated cells was present at early stopping.

\section{Real-data case study: electrolyte conductivity}\label{sec:5}

\textbf{Task and model.} The CALiSol-23 challenge \citep{deblasio2024calisol} asks for the log conductivity of lithium-ion electrolytes; every test sample contains diethyl carbonate (DEC), which never appears in training. KAN-$\delta$ anchors each prediction on the measured conductivity of pure propylene carbonate (PC) and learns only the correction, as in $\Delta$-machine learning \citep{ramakrishnan2015delta}, $\log k = \log k_{\mathrm{PC}} + x_{\mathrm{co}}\, h(z)$, where h is a FastKAN-style network of shape [10, 6, 1]. Its inputs are physical descriptors of the solvents (dielectric constant, log viscosity, molar mass), temperature, molality and a salt embedding. A second-difference penalty acts on the RBF coefficients, and the SiLU weights are unpenalised. Early-stopped after 107 AdamW epochs, it reached RMSE 0.142 on a held-out co-solvent (fold A: ethyl acetate held out). Its AdamW weight decay played no part: retraining without it left the early-stopped norms essentially unchanged and fold A's RMSE at 0.1420 (a two-sided pre-registered prediction whose verdict was the branch "incidental").

\textbf{The inputs are correlated and few-valued.} The three co-solvent descriptors take only 30 distinct combinations in training, and dielectric constant and log viscosity correlate at r = 0.966.

\textbf{Nothing ever converged.}

\begin{itemize}
  \item Of 190 pairs of polished independent seeds, none computed the same function.
  \item After 20,000 float64 L-BFGS iterations (the "capped" state used below), 0 of 26 models converged; exact-Hessian trust-region methods also failed on every seed.
  \item Students trained on a frozen teacher matched its predictions (correlation 0.9988) but not its hidden units (0.66).
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The anatomy matches Section 3.}

\begin{itemize}
  \item From early stopping to the capped state, the squared parameter norm grew 150--1550$\times$ while the smoothness penalty fell 8--88$\times$.
  \item At least 99.9\% of the coefficient change during exact-Newton polishing lay in the penalty's affine null space, in 9 of 9 models.
  \item Cancellation within an edge (SiLU against RBF) stayed small, 1.13--1.33. Cancellation across the edges entering a unit rose from 1.7--2.9 to 4--10, consistent with the correlated descriptors.
  \item The runaway spread across both layers: 30--40\% of the parameter change went into layer-1 affine RBF coefficients, 37--38\% into SiLU weights and 19--31\% into layer-2 affine coefficients (post-hoc), and 12--39\% of hidden units saturated. In the synthetic runaway the output layer dominated.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Extrapolation suffered.} Polishing beyond early stopping under a weak null-space penalty ($\mu$ = $10^{-6}$) raised fold A's RMSE from 0.142 to 1.03 (0.33 under the stronger penalty $\mu$ = $10^{-4}$; Section 9). Fold A's co-solvent lies outside the training data's descriptor hull (Figure~\ref{fig:applicability}c), although on the correlation pattern of dielectric constant and viscosity. Within the fold, the damage scales with the co-solvent fraction: the learned correction enters as $x_{\mathrm{co}}\, h$, so any change polishing makes to h is magnified where $x_{\mathrm{co}}$ is large (descriptive; Figure~\ref{fig:applicability}a, b). Across the co-solvent folds with at least 20 test rows, no distance measure distinguishably predicted where errors were large, and a planned predictive follow-up was dropped because its pre-stated precondition was not met. The degradation was much stronger than in the synthetic study, where correlation itself caused most of the off-pattern error; possible reasons include the larger model, its larger norm growth, and a held-out solvent outside the descriptor hull.

\section{Is the minimum at infinity?}\label{sec:6}

Failing to converge does not by itself show that the loss has no finite minimum. The minimum could be finite but very far away, or the problem could simply be too ill-conditioned for the optimiser to finish. Two pre-registered experiments separate these possibilities: freezing one layer, and following a certified regularisation path.

\textbf{Freezing a layer.} With the first layer frozen at its early-stopped weights, only the output layer is trained. Its parameters enter the output linearly, so the penalised loss is a convex quadratic. Every model then reached a certified minimum: 6 of 6 real KAN-$\delta$ seeds and 8 of 8 in each correlated synthetic cell, with no negative curvature at any logged iterate; a one-layer KAN trained on correlated inputs also certified, 8 of 8. The pre-registered prediction that the norm would grow at most threefold failed: the real models grew a median $\times$583 to reach their minima. That growth is not a runaway, because it ends at a certified point. Freezing the second layer instead leaves a non-convex problem. The synthetic models still certified (16 of 16), but the real first layer grew by factors of $10^{4}$ to $10^{10}$, mostly through cancellation across its edges, and its endpoints were highly degenerate, with 21--41 near-flat directions; one endpoint that passed the certificate turned out, on a longer restart, to be still drifting outward (exploratory arm; post-hoc follow-up). Section 3 draws the conclusion: the runaway needs trained parameters acting through a nonlinearity, and whether such a problem degenerates depends on the data.

\textbf{A certified regularisation path.} For a loss L that is bounded below and a penalty R that grows without bound with the parameters, the global minimisers of $L + \gamma R$ stay bounded as $\gamma \to 0$ if and only if L has a finite minimiser. We use R = $\|\theta\|^{2}$ over all parameters, follow $\gamma$ from $10^{-2}$ down to $10^{-7}$ in half-decade steps, warm-start each value from the previous solution, and certify every point; degenerate points are accepted only after probes for remaining descent. On synthetic data, with the blind spot open, the minimisers' squared norm grew as a power of 1/$\gamma$ (exponent 0.63--0.76 under P0, 0.36 under P1) while the unregularised loss kept falling; with the null space closed (P2), the path levelled off (exponent 0.014, ratio 1.004 between the two smallest $\gamma$). On the six real models, the same divergence appeared on six distinct branches: exponents 0.74--0.88, squared norms reaching 596--3052, and the unregularised loss falling from 2.05$\cdot10^{-2}$ to 8.7--9.3$\cdot10^{-3}$. All pre-registered predictions held, the real-data discrimination check being taken from the synthetic controls as pre-registered. (Figure~\ref{fig:paths})

  \caption{Certified $L_2$ regularisation paths, $\gamma = 10^{-2}$ to $10^{-7}$ in half-decade steps (warm-started), one line per seed. \textbf{(a, c)} Synthetic correlated inputs, 8 seeds per penalty level: $\|\theta^*\|^2$ grows as a power of $1/\gamma$ with exponent 0.63--0.76 (P0) and 0.36 (P1), and 0.014 with the null space closed (P2). \textbf{(b, d)} Real data: the 6 KAN-$\delta$ seeds with the blind spot open (exponents 0.74--0.88) and seeds ind0 and ind1 with the null-space penalty at $\mu = 10^{-4}$ (post-hoc control, outcomes fixed in advance; ratio between the two smallest $\gamma$ 1.09 and 1.10). $L^*$ is the loss without the $\gamma$ term (for the closed paths, including $\mu Q$). Filled markers: points included in the pre-registered fits; open markers: reached but not included; absent: not reached.}
  \label{fig:paths}
\end{figure}

Two details matter for how far these replicate. On synthetic data the warm-started paths start from nearly one function; under P1 and P2 they stay together along the whole path, while under P0 they separate into a few branches. The real paths, by contrast, are genuinely distinct and compute different functions: at $\gamma$ $\leq$ $10^{-4}$ their predictions differ by a median 13.7--16.3\% of the output's standard deviation.

\textbf{Robustness (post hoc).} Polishing from independent cold starts found no small-norm basin at any $\gamma$; at $\gamma$ = $10^{-7}$ under P1, 8 of 9 cold starts reached a \emph{lower} regularised objective than the warm path, at a larger norm. The warm path therefore understates the divergence. A straight line along the final drift direction rises almost at once: the minimisers recede along a curved valley, not along a ray. The growth sits in the penalty's blind directions, the affine RBF coefficients and SiLU weights of both layers, while the curved coefficients and the salt embedding shrink.

\textbf{Closing the null space on real data.} In a control whose two possible outcomes were fixed in advance, the same path on the real loss with the null-space penalty at $\mu$ = $10^{-4}$ levelled off: squared norms of 27.7 and 27.4 against 596 and 2200 for the same seeds with the blind spot open (ratios 1.09 and 1.10). The plateau is not a full stop: the norm still creeps up (whole-path exponents 0.105 and 0.124), in the biases, the curved RBF coefficients and the salt embedding, which this penalty leaves weakly penalised or free. The price is a higher training loss: +6\% and +23\% for the two seeds (1.0926$\cdot10^{-2}$ against 1.0300$\cdot10^{-2}$, and 1.1224$\cdot10^{-2}$ against 9.113$\cdot10^{-3}$). When the penalty is instead lowered towards zero, the growth floods whichever parameters it leaves free: with the null-space penalty of Section 3 the salt embedding grows 44--218-fold, while a variant that also penalises biases and embeddings keeps the embedding bounded.

\textbf{Reading.} Over the tested range, $\gamma$ = $10^{-2}$ to $10^{-7}$, the loss with the blind spot open behaves as if its infimum lies at infinity, on synthetic and real data alike, and closing the null space bounds it. Two limits apply: the criterion concerns global minimisers while the path follows one local branch, and a finite minimum lying beyond the tested range cannot be excluded. The conclusions are stated for that range only.

\section{How much correlation does the blind spot need?}\label{sec:7}

Section 4 compared two doses, independent inputs and $\rho$ = 0.95. A pre-registered dose-response study fills in between: $\rho$ $\in$ \{0, 0.5, 0.8, 0.9, 0.95, 0.99\} for both input pairs, P0 and P1 at every level, 8 seeds each, with paired random draws so that only the correlation changes, plus the null-space control P2 at $\rho$ = 0.99. A replication gate ran first: the new $\rho$ = 0.95 cells reproduced the committed synthetic study bit for bit.

\textbf{Correlation drives non-convergence.} The share of models that fail to certify rises with $\rho$ (prediction held; P0 with one allowed inversion). It first exceeds one half at $\rho$ = 0.5 under P0 and at $\rho$ = 0.9 under P1, and from $\rho$ = 0.95 no model certifies under either penalty. These thresholds belong to this synthetic setting ([4, 3, 1], Gaussian inputs); they are not thresholds for real data. With the null space closed, all 8 models certify even at $\rho$ = 0.99, and a short regularisation path levels off (median D = 1.13, defined below). Along with the dose, the hidden units become correlated (largest pairwise correlation from about 0.05 at $\rho$ = 0 to 0.82--0.96 at $\rho$ $\geq$ 0.9), and the polished training loss falls (Spearman $-$0.94): more correlation lets the runaway buy more loss. (Figure~\ref{fig:corrdose})


\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig6_correlation_dose.pdf}
  % CAPTION-DRAFT: review (numbers from paper2/figures/fig6_correlation_dose.json)
  \caption{Correlation dose-response (synthetic [4, 3, 1], Gaussian inputs; 8 seeds per cell; the thresholds are synthetic, not real-data thresholds). Horizontal axis: $\rho$ on a $\log 1/(1-\rho)$ scale. \textbf{(a)} Share of models not certified (dashed: one half). \textbf{(b)} Median short-path $D = \|\theta^*(10^{-7})\|^2/\|\theta^*(10^{-5})\|^2$ (log scale; dashed: 1.5). \textbf{(c)} Largest hidden-unit correlation, cell median. Diamonds: P2 at $\rho = 0.99$, 8 of 8 certified, median $D = 1.13$.}
  \label{fig:corrdose}
\end{figure}

\textbf{What a short path cannot tell.} We also predicted that a short regularisation path ($\gamma$ = $10^{-3}$, $10^{-5}$, $10^{-7}$), summarised by D = $\|\theta^{*}$($10^{-7}$)$\|^{2}$ / $\|\theta^{*}$($10^{-5}$)$\|^{2}$, would diverge more strongly as $\rho$ grows. It did not (Spearman 0.71 under P0 and 0.14 under P1, against the required 0.8): D was already high at every dose, including $\rho$ = 0. A post-hoc check, with its classification rule fixed before computing, explains why. Where the unregularised polish certified, mostly at low $\rho$, 30 of 32 paths were heading towards that certified finite minimum or its valley, none moved outward past it, and 2 found a better minimum at smaller norm. Along one direction with curvature $\lambda$, $D = \bigl((\lambda + 2\gamma_1)/(\lambda + 2\gamma_2)\bigr)^{2}$ with $\gamma_{1}$ = $10^{-5}$ and $\gamma_{2}$ = $10^{-7}$, so a finite minimum whose curvature lies within or near the window 2$\cdot10^{-7}$ to 2$\cdot10^{-5}$ keeps D large while the path is still approaching it; the observed low-$\rho$ medians (4.54 to 15.05) correspond to $\lambda$ = 6.7$\cdot10^{-6}$ to 1.7$\cdot10^{-5}$. A two-decade D therefore cannot separate a distant finite minimum from a receding one. The receding minimum of Section 6 is established at $\rho$ = 0.95 and on the real data; at low $\rho$ the minima are finite but distant; at intermediate $\rho$ these tests do not settle the question. A secondary prediction, that the affine share of the parameter change would rise steadily with $\rho$, failed.

\section{Is it the basis?}\label{sec:8}

The experiments so far use Gaussian-RBF edges. To test whether the runaway belongs to the basis or to the penalty's blind spot, we replicated the synthetic 2$\times$3 study with cubic B-spline edges as in pykan and efficient-kan: uniform knots with G = 5 intervals on [$-$1, 1], extended by three knots at each end, giving 8 basis functions per edge (matching the 8 Gaussians), plus the SiLU term. On these knots, constant and linear coefficient patterns reproduce constant and linear functions exactly, so the second-difference penalty's blind spot is exactly the affine functions. The teacher was refitted into the B-spline basis; inputs, seeds and noise were those of the RBF study.

\textbf{The runaway carries over.} With correlated inputs, none of the 16 P0 and P1 models certified (prediction held; Figure~\ref{fig:bspline}a). The runaway is a property of the penalty's affine null space, not of the Gaussian basis.

\textbf{The fix carries over, with a lesson about calibration.} The null-space weight was set by the same committed rule as in the RBF study (the smallest $\mu$ whose pilot models grew at most threefold), which here chose $\mu$ = $10^{-6}$, the bottom of the grid, against $10^{-5}$ for RBF edges. At that weight, the closed models certified 8 of 8 in both conditions, but the pre-registered bound on the short path failed with correlated inputs (median D = 2.23 against 1.5). Post-hoc checks, with predictions fixed in advance, traced this to the measurement window: the null-space penalty's curvature, about 1.8$\mu$, lies between the two $\gamma$ values that D compares. Extended to $\gamma$ = $10^{-9}$, the paths were bounded (Figure~\ref{fig:bspline}b, c), ending near the certified minima's norm though not always at the same point; and at the RBF study's $\mu$ = $10^{-5}$ the fix met the original standard (8 of 8 certified, D = 1.17 and 1.31). The growth-based rule chose a weight too small for a criterion carried over from another setting: a lesson about calibration, not about the fix.


\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig7_bspline.pdf}
  % CAPTION-DRAFT: review (numbers from paper2/figures/fig7_bspline.json)
  \caption{B-spline replication. \textbf{(a)} Certified models (of 8) per cell: the Gaussian-RBF study (frozen $\mu = 10^{-5}$) and the cubic B-spline replication (frozen $\mu = 10^{-6}$). \textbf{(b, c)} P2 regularisation paths at $\mu = 10^{-6}$, continued to $\gamma = 10^{-9}$ (post hoc, predictions fixed in advance): $\|\theta^*(\gamma)\|$ relative to each seed's certified polish minimum; shaded: the pre-fixed band [0.9, 1.1]. Median ratio at $\gamma = 10^{-9}$: 1.000 (independent) and 0.911 (correlated).}
  \label{fig:bspline}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Independent inputs.} Fewer independent models certified than with RBF edges (5 and 4 of 8 under P0 and P1, against 6), so the pre-registered prediction failed, and its fixed reading applies: the B-spline basis is less benign on independent inputs. Post hoc, two of the seven failures look like runaways, one like slow convergence, and four are mixed; with 8 models per cell, the margin is one or two models.

\textbf{A symmetry the RBFs lack.} Because B-splines sum exactly to one, constants can be moved between a unit's incoming edges and its bias without changing the loss: an exact 15-dimensional symmetry in the [4, 3, 1] model, which holds only approximately for RBF edges. It made the solver hang at converged points and would have made every certified point look degenerate. We excluded these analytically constructed directions, never fitted ones, from certification and from the degeneracy count; exact symmetries are redundancy in the parameterisation, while the runaway directions, which are approximate and data-dependent, remain subject to every check. This was one of five changes to the study's calibration step made after outcomes were known; none touched a prediction, a threshold or an interpretation rule, and all are listed in Appendix D.

\textbf{A known solution becomes recoverable.} Under the regularised loss, the original teacher is no longer a minimum. Optimising it under the same loss gives a "regularised teacher" computing nearly the same function (correlation 0.9992). Students match its units at 0.87--0.90 and its edges at 0.97--0.98, against 0.68--0.72 and 0.84--0.91 for the original teacher. This comparison was defined after the results and is exploratory.

\textbf{The penalty acts partly as gauge fixing.} At the certified minima, the layer-2 constant shift, an essentially exact symmetry, owes 96\% of its curvature to $\mu Q$: the regulariser selects one representative. The layer-1 constant shift (46\%) and unit rescaling (24\%) are only approximate symmetries in this architecture, because Gaussian bumps cannot represent constants exactly and tanh breaks rescaling.

\textbf{Convergence is not uniqueness.} Independent seeds at certified minima still disagreed: their median prediction difference fell by only 26\% (Figure~\ref{fig:uniqueness}b). With the runaway removed, the loss has several distinct isolated minima.

Groups marked $^*$ (polished fold A) are not in any committed result: they were evaluated post hoc from the archived polished weights (SHA-verified; predictions on the 1434 fold A training rows), without any re-optimisation.}
  \label{fig:uniqueness}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Three kinds of flatness.} Certification needs care at flat points. Exact symmetries of the parameterisation, such as the constant shifts of B-spline edges (Section 8), are flat by construction and harmless; we exclude them analytically. Near-flat directions from poor conditioning are not harmless: certified points with many of them can be degenerate, and in one real-data case a point that passed the certificate kept descending on a longer restart while its squared norm grew 6.7-fold. The runaway valley itself is approximate and data-dependent. We therefore report the number of near-flat directions with every certificate, and probe degenerate points for remaining descent before counting them as minima. Certified, in short, is not the same as unique, and not necessarily the same as good: some certified minima lie at higher loss than points the regularisation path finds at smaller norm.

\textbf{Extrapolation.} On the held-out co-solvent, RMSE was 0.142 for the early-stopped model, 1.026 after polishing at $\mu$ = $10^{-6}$ and 0.33 at $\mu$ = $10^{-4}$. Bounding the runaway recovers most of the damage, but early stopping remains the most accurate choice: on an ill-conditioned problem, stopping early keeps the poorly determined directions near their starting values, much as ridge regularisation would \citep{yao2007early,ali2019continuous}.

\textbf{Structured alternatives.} We tested two architectures designed to remove runaway routes by construction, against the early-stopped baseline, with leave-one-co-solvent-out (LOCO) validation:

Seed agreement is the median prediction difference between seeds (lower is better). The shared-curve model converged every time, ending with no near-flat directions where the baseline had a median of 106 (range 86--116, at non-stationary points; Figure~\ref{fig:uniqueness}a), and it was less accurate. At the early-stopped state its seeds agreed less than the baseline's (the pre-registered comparison); after polishing to certified minima their median disagreement fell to 0.085, with some seed pairs reaching the same minimum (post-hoc). The excess model's "pure co-solvent offset" tracked viscosity rather than dielectric constant (rank correlation $-$0.85, post hoc), reflecting that no training row contains a pure co-solvent.

\section{Recommendations for practitioners}\label{sec:10}

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Penalise the blind spot, and everything else that is free.} If a KAN uses a second-difference or curvature penalty, add a small penalty on the constant-plus-linear component of each edge's coefficients and on each SiLU weight, in every layer, and give biases and embeddings a small penalty too: penalising only part of the free directions redirects the growth into the rest. This restores bounded minima, not the accuracy of early stopping.
  \item \textbf{Calibrate that penalty by certification and a plateau, not by growth.} Choose its weight so that models certify and the regularisation path levels off; a rule based on norm growth chose a weight too small in our B-spline replication.
  \item \textbf{Check input correlations, including between hidden units.} Strongly correlated or few-valued inputs make a trained nonlinear layer vulnerable, and hidden units that become correlated expose the next layer.
  \item \textbf{Judge convergence by certification, not by norms or the loss.} Large growth can end at a finite minimum; a runaway is growth that never reaches a certified one. Report the number of near-flat directions with every certificate, and probe degenerate points before calling them minima.
  \item \textbf{Do not read edges from unconverged models.} Compare edges across seeds only after removing exact symmetries, and only for models at certified minima.
  \item \textbf{Treat seed disagreement as information.} Even at certified minima, distinct solutions remain; disagreement then signals that the data do not determine the function, not merely that training was unfinished.
  \item \textbf{Validate on genuinely new conditions, and keep early stopping as a baseline.} A held-out fold from the training distribution can understate extrapolation error severalfold; in our real-data case, early stopping gave the best held-out accuracy of every variant tested.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Limitations and research process}\label{sec:11}

\textbf{Scope.}

\begin{itemize}
  \item One real dataset and one synthetic teacher; small networks ([4, 3, 1] and [10, 6, 1]).
  \item Two edge types: Gaussian RBFs on fixed centres and cubic B-splines on a fixed uniform grid, each with a SiLU base. Grid updates and other penalty families were not tested.
  \item Our P1 keeps the second-difference penalty and adds Bagrow's SiLU term; it is Bagrow-style, not a replication of his RBF curvature form.
  \item The receding minimum is established over $\gamma$ = $10^{-2}$ to $10^{-7}$ only, at $\rho$ = 0.95 and on the real data; the dose thresholds are synthetic.
  \item The null-space weight in the shared-curve model was carried over from the synthetic calibration, not re-calibrated.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Post-hoc elements.} The second-order certificate, the regularised-teacher comparison, the gauge-curvature analysis, the anatomy studies, the loss decomposition, the degeneracy probes, the cold starts, the dose-response settling check and the B-spline follow-up checks were defined after seeing results. We report them as exploratory and never in place of pre-registered verdicts; where their rules were fixed before computing, we say so.

\textbf{Amendments and dropped work.} Five changes to the B-spline study's calibration step were made after outcomes were known (Appendix D); none changed a prediction, a threshold or an interpretation rule. A planned predictive follow-up to the applicability analysis was dropped because its pre-stated precondition was not met.

\textbf{Extrapolation.} The strong degradation from polishing appeared on real data but not in the synthetic study, so we do not claim it as a general law.

\textbf{Process.} Each study committed its predictions, thresholds and interpretation rules before its code existed; any later change was dated and recorded as an amendment, and every verdict is linked to the commit that produced it. Several predictions failed or proved untestable as specified; following them up, rather than reinterpreting them, is what led to the mechanism reported here. Experiments were run with an AI coding agent working under this protocol, with a rule that committed files take precedence over any number stated in a prompt.
